subject: maths
title: Chance: Certain, Likely, Unlikely or Impossible
seo_title: Year 3 Chance Worksheets: Certain, Likely, Unlikely, Impossible (Free, with Answers)
standard_text: Identify practical activities and everyday events involving chance; describe possible outcomes and events as ‘likely’ or ‘unlikely’ and identify some events as ‘certain’ or ‘impossible’ explaining reasoning
meta_desc: Free Year 3 maths worksheets on chance: describe everyday events as certain, likely, unlikely or impossible, compare colours on spinners and in bags of counters, list the outcomes of a dice or coin, and read the results of chance experiments. 100 questions with an answer key, aligned to the Australian Curriculum (AC9M3P01, AC9M3P02). Useful NAPLAN numeracy practice.
key_big: Impossible means it can never happen. Unlikely means it could happen, but probably will not.
key_sub: Certain means it must happen. On a spinner or in a bag, the colour that covers more is more likely. Every number on a dice is equally likely, and results change each time you repeat an experiment.
body_html:
The chance words

Chance is how likely something is to happen. We use four words. Impossible means it can never happen. Certain means it must happen. In between are unlikely (it could happen, but not often) and likely (it will probably happen).

WordMeaningExample
certainmust happenThe sun will rise tomorrow.
likelywill probably happenIt will be warm on a summer day in Sydney.
unlikelycould happen, but probably will notA koala will walk into the classroom.
impossiblecan never happenIt will snow in Darwin in summer.

Spinners: look at the size of each part

A spinner is more likely to land on a colour that covers more of it. Compare the size of the parts, not just the number of sections.

Example

Which colour is the arrow most likely to land on?

Red covers 3 sections. Blue covers 1 section.

Answer: red

Bags of counters

When you pick without looking, the colour with more counters is more likely. If every counter is one colour, that colour is certain. If a colour is not in the bag, it is impossible.

Example

Is picking a blue counter unlikely or impossible?

There is 1 blue counter, so it could happen. It is not impossible.

Answer: unlikely

Possible outcomes

An outcome is something that can happen. A coin has 2 outcomes: heads or tails. A dice has 6 outcomes: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. Each face has the same chance, so all 6 numbers are equally likely.

Example

Is rolling a 7 on a dice unlikely or impossible?

A dice only shows 1 to 6.

Answer: impossible

Chance experiments

Do the same thing many times and keep a tally. The results vary: if you do it again, you will probably get different numbers. A big part of a spinner usually comes up more often.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Saying impossible when it is only unlikelyIf it could happen even once, it is not impossible
Choosing your favourite colourLook at how much of the spinner or bag is that colour
Thinking a 6 is harder to roll than a 1Every number on a dice is equally likely
Counting sections, not their sizeCompare how much of the spinner each colour covers
Expecting the same results every timeResults change each time you repeat an experiment
Thinking tails is due after many headsA coin does not remember: heads and tails stay equally likely

faq.q: What do Year 3 students learn about chance?
faq.a: In the Australian Curriculum (AC9M3P01 and AC9M3P02), Year 3 students describe events as certain, likely, unlikely or impossible and explain why. They also list possible outcomes, run simple chance experiments and see that results vary.

faq.q: What is the difference between unlikely and impossible?
faq.a: Unlikely means it could happen, but probably will not, like picking the one blue counter from a bag of ten. Impossible means it can never happen, like rolling a 7 on a dice.

faq.q: How do you know which colour a spinner is most likely to land on?
faq.a: Look at how much of the spinner each colour covers. The colour with the biggest part is most likely, even if another colour has more small sections.

faq.q: Why do the results change when you repeat a chance experiment?
faq.a: Each spin, roll or toss is up to chance, so the results are a little different every time. Over many tries, the results usually match the chances, such as about half heads with a coin.

sets.title: Everyday events: certain, likely, unlikely or impossible?

items.q: The sun will rise tomorrow morning. This is …
items.e: The sun rises every morning. It always happens, so it is certain.

items.q: It will snow in Darwin this summer. This is …
items.e: Darwin is in the hot tropical north. Summer there is hot and wet, and snow does not fall in Darwin, so it is impossible.

items.q: After Wednesday, the next day will be Thursday. This is …
items.e: The days of the week always come in the same order. Thursday always comes after Wednesday, so it is certain.

items.q: A kangaroo will fly over the school like a bird. This is …
items.e: Kangaroos hop, but they cannot fly. This can never happen, so it is impossible.

items.q: Oliver is 8. Next year he will be 9. This is …
items.e: Everyone is one year older each year. 8 + 1 = 9, so it is certain.

items.q: Tomorrow will have 30 hours. This is …
items.e: Every day has 24 hours. A day can never have 30 hours, so it is impossible.

items.q: It will be cold on a winter morning in Canberra. This is …
items.e: Canberra winter mornings are usually very cold, often below 0 °C. Most of the time this happens, but a mild morning is possible, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: Mia will find a $50 note on the way to school. This is …
items.e: It could happen, but it almost never does. So it is unlikely. It is not impossible: notes do get dropped.

items.q: It will be warm on a January day at the beach in Sydney. This is …
items.e: January is summer in Australia, so most days are warm. A few days can be cool or rainy, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: A koala will walk into the classroom today. This is …
items.e: Koalas live in trees in the bush. One could wander into a school, but it hardly ever happens. So it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: If Isla drops a tennis ball, it will fall down. This is …
items.e: When you let go of a ball, it always falls to the ground. It must happen, so it is certain.

items.q: It will rain every day in January in Perth. This is …
items.e: January is summer in Perth. Most January days are dry and sunny, so rain on every single day is unlikely.

items.q: Leo is 8. Next year he will be 3 years old. This is …
items.e: You cannot get younger. Next year Leo will be 9, so being 3 is impossible.

items.q: The next vehicle that drives past the school will have 4 wheels. This is …
items.e: Most vehicles on the road are cars with 4 wheels. But the next one could be a motorbike or a truck, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: Ruby will drink some water at school today. This is …
items.e: Most students drink water during a school day. Ruby could forget, so it is likely, not certain.

items.q: Jack will roll a 6 on a dice five times in a row. This is …
items.e: Rolling a 6 once is unlikely (1 out of 6 faces). Five 6s in a row is even harder. It could happen, so it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Which event is certain?
c: Kai will have pasta for dinner
Ava will win her race at the athletics carnival
items.e: Friday always comes after Thursday, so it is certain. Rain, winning a race and pasta for dinner might happen, but they might not.

items.q: Which event is impossible?
c: Lachlan will see a bird today
Grace will lose a tooth this year
It will be sunny on Saturday
A cat will fly to the Moon
items.e: A cat cannot fly, and it cannot get to the Moon, so this can never happen. The other events could happen.

items.q: Which event is unlikely?
c: A fish will ride a bike
A snake will be found in the school library
Students will eat lunch at school today
items.e: A snake in the library could happen, but it is rare, so it is unlikely. The sun setting is certain, a fish riding a bike is impossible, and students eating lunch is likely.

items.q: Only 2 of the 20 students will be picked for the netball team. Chloe says, “It is impossible that I will be picked.” Which word should she use instead?
items.e: 2 of the 20 students will be picked, so Chloe could be one of them. It is possible, but not very likely. The right word is unlikely, not impossible.

sets.title: Spinners: which colour is most likely?

items.q: The spinner has 4 equal sections. Which colour is the arrow most likely to land on?
c: red and blue are equally likely
items.e: 3 of the 4 equal sections are red and only 1 is blue, so red is most likely. (There is no green, so green is impossible.)

items.q: The spinner has 6 equal sections. Which colour is the arrow least likely to land on?
items.e: Only 1 of the 6 equal sections is green. 5 are yellow. Green has the smallest part, so it is least likely.

items.q: Landing on red is …
items.e: Every section is red. The arrow must land on red, so it is certain.

items.q: Landing on red is …
items.e: Only 1 of the 6 equal sections is red. It can happen, but not often, so it is unlikely. It is not impossible, because there is a red section.

items.q: Landing on green is …
items.e: There is no green section on this spinner. The arrow can never land on green, so it is impossible.

items.q: Landing on green is …
items.e: 5 of the 6 equal sections are green, so green is likely. It is not certain, because there is 1 purple section.

items.q: Which colour can the arrow never land on?
items.e: The spinner has red, blue and yellow sections only. There is no green, so landing on green is impossible.

items.q: Which colour is the arrow most likely to land on?
c: all three colours are equally likely
items.e: Look at the size of each part, not the number of sections. Blue is one big section: half of the spinner. Red is 2 small sections (a quarter) and yellow is 2 small sections (a quarter). So blue is most likely.

items.q: Which two colours are equally likely?
items.e: Red and green are each a quarter of the spinner. Parts of the same size are equally likely. Yellow is half of the spinner, so it is more likely than red or green.

items.q: Landing on yellow is …
items.e: Yellow is only a quarter of the spinner and green is three quarters. Yellow can happen, but it is unlikely.

items.q: The spinner has 8 equal sections. Which number is the arrow most likely to land on?
c: all the numbers are equally likely
items.e: All 8 sections are the same size, so each number has the same chance. A bigger number is not harder or easier to get.

items.q: Landing on a number less than 5 is …
items.e: The numbers on the spinner are 1, 2, 3 and 4. They are all less than 5, so it is certain.

items.q: Landing on 7 is …
items.e: The numbers go from 1 to 6. There is no 7 on the spinner, so it is impossible.

items.q: Which spinner is certain to land on blue?
items.e: Spinner B is all blue, so it must land on blue. Spinner C is likely to land on blue, but it could land on yellow, so it is not certain.

items.q: On which spinner is landing on red impossible?
items.e: Spinner D has no red section, so red is impossible there. Spinner A has 1 red section: red is unlikely there, but not impossible.

items.q: On which spinner is landing on red most likely?
items.e: Compare how much of each spinner is red. C is three quarters red. D has 3 red sections, but they are small: together they are less than half of the spinner.

items.q: On which spinner are red and blue equally likely?
items.e: Spinner A is half red and half blue, so red and blue are equally likely. In C, red and blue each have 1 section, but the red section is bigger, so red is more likely there.

items.q: Ethan colours a spinner with 4 equal sections. He wants landing on red to be unlikely, but not impossible. How many sections should he colour red?
items.e: 1 red section out of 4 makes red unlikely. 0 red sections would make red impossible. 3 would make it likely, and 4 would make it certain.

items.q: Sienna says the arrow will probably land on yellow, because yellow is her favourite colour. Which colour is the arrow more likely to land on?
c: it is certain to land on yellow
items.e: Your favourite colour does not change the chance. 6 of the 8 equal sections are green and 2 are yellow, so green is more likely.

items.q: Put the colours in order from most likely to least likely.
items.e: Count the equal sections: red 3, blue 2, yellow 1. The most sections is most likely, so the order is red, blue, yellow.

sets.title: Bags of counters: what could you pick?

items.q: Zara picks one counter from the bag without looking. Which colour is she most likely to pick?
c: red and blue are equally likely
items.e: There are 6 red counters and only 2 blue counters. More red counters means red is more likely.

items.q: Noah picks one counter without looking. Which colour is he least likely to pick?
items.e: There is only 1 green counter and 7 yellow counters, so green is least likely.

items.q: Picking a blue counter from this bag is …
items.e: Every counter in the bag is blue, so you must pick blue. It is certain.

items.q: Picking a green counter from this bag is …
items.e: There are only red and yellow counters. There is no green counter, so it is impossible.

items.q: Picking a red counter from this bag is …
items.e: 7 of the 8 counters are red, so red is likely. It is not certain, because there is 1 blue counter.

items.q: Picking a red counter from this bag is …
items.e: Only 1 of the 10 counters is red. It can happen, but not often, so it is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Which colour is impossible to pick from this bag?
items.e: The bag has red, blue and yellow counters. There is no green, so green is impossible. There is 1 yellow counter, so yellow is unlikely, not impossible.

items.q: Which sentence is true?
c: Red is more likely than blue
Red and blue are equally likely
items.e: There are 4 red and 4 blue counters. The same number of each colour means they are equally likely.

items.q: This bag has 9 green marbles and 1 purple marble. Harper picks one marble without looking. Picking the purple marble is …
items.e: Only 1 of the 10 marbles is purple. It can happen, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Which two colours are equally likely to be picked?
items.e: There are 3 red, 3 blue and 2 yellow counters. Red and blue have the same number, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Put the colours in order from most likely to least likely.
items.e: Count each colour: yellow 5, red 2, green 1. The most counters is most likely: yellow, red, green.

items.q: Mei takes all the blue counters out of the bag. Now picking a red counter is …
items.e: After the blue counters come out, only the 3 red counters are left. You must pick red, so it is certain.

items.q: Kai puts 6 more green counters into the bag. Which colour is now more likely to be picked?
items.e: Green: 2 + 6 = 8 counters. Red: 6 counters. 8 is more than 6, so green is now more likely.

items.q: Which bag makes picking a red counter certain?
items.e: Bag D has only red counters, so red is certain. Bag B is likely to give red, but not certain, because it has 1 blue counter.

items.q: From which bag is picking a yellow counter impossible?
items.e: Bag A has no yellow counters, so yellow is impossible. Bag B has 1 yellow counter, so yellow is unlikely there, not impossible.

items.q: From which bag is picking a blue counter most likely?
items.e: Each bag has 6 counters. Bag B has the most blue counters (5), so blue is most likely there.

items.q: From which bag is picking a red counter unlikely (but not impossible)?
items.e: Bag C has only 1 red counter out of 6, so red is unlikely. Bag D has no red, so red is impossible there. A is certain and B is likely.

items.q: Ruby’s bag has 3 red counters and 2 blue counters. She wants picking a blue counter to be impossible. What should she do?
items.e: Impossible means it can never happen. If there are no blue counters left, blue can never be picked. Adding red counters only makes blue unlikely.

items.q: A bag has 10 counters. Picking a red counter is certain. How many red counters are in the bag?
items.e: Certain means it must happen, so every counter must be red: all 10. With 9 red and 1 other counter, red is likely, not certain.

items.q: At the school fete lucky dip there are 20 prizes: 15 lolly bags, 4 pencils and 1 toy car. Grace picks one prize without looking. Which prize is she most likely to get?
items.e: 15 of the 20 prizes are lolly bags. That is more than all the others, so a lolly bag is most likely. There is only 1 toy car, so it is unlikely.

sets.title: Dice, coins and number cards: possible outcomes

items.q: Isla tosses a coin. What are the possible outcomes?
items.e: A coin has two sides: heads and tails. It can land on either one, so the outcomes are heads or tails.

items.q: Oliver rolls a dice. What are all the possible outcomes?
items.e: A dice has 6 faces with 1 to 6 dots. Any face can land on top: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. There is no 0.

items.q: How many different outcomes are there when you roll a dice?
items.e: The outcomes are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. That is 6 outcomes.

items.q: Which number is impossible to roll on a dice?
items.e: A dice shows 1 to 6. There is no 7, so rolling a 7 is impossible.

items.q: Rolling a number less than 7 on a dice is …
items.e: Every number on a dice (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) is less than 7. It must happen, so it is certain.

items.q: Rolling a number greater than 6 on a dice is …
items.e: The biggest number on a dice is 6. You can never roll more than 6, so it is impossible.

items.q: Rolling a 6 on a dice is …
items.e: Only 1 of the 6 faces shows 6. It can happen, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Rolling a number greater than 1 on a dice is …
items.e: 5 of the 6 faces are greater than 1 (2, 3, 4, 5, 6). Only the 1 is not. So it is likely.

items.q: Noah thinks a 6 is harder to roll than a 1, because 6 is a bigger number. Is he right?
items.e: Each face of a dice has the same chance. The size of the number does not matter. 1 and 6 are each 1 face out of 6, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Charlotte tosses a coin. Getting heads is …
items.e: A coin has one heads side and one tails side, so heads and tails are equally likely.

items.q: How many different outcomes (colours) can this spinner land on?
items.e: The spinner has 4 sections, but two of them are red. The different colours are red, blue and green: 3 outcomes. (Counting sections gives 4.)

items.q: Matilda has number cards from 1 to 10. She turns them face down and picks one. Which number is impossible to pick?
items.e: The cards go from 1 to 10. There is no 11 card, so 11 is impossible.

items.q: Number cards 1 to 10 are face down. Picking a number less than 11 is …
items.e: Every card from 1 to 10 is less than 11. It must happen, so it is certain.

items.q: Number cards 1 to 10 are face down. Picking a number greater than 2 is …
items.e: 8 of the 10 cards are greater than 2 (3 to 10). Only 1 and 2 are not. So it is likely.

items.q: Number cards 1 to 10 are face down. Picking the 10 is …
items.e: There is only 1 card with 10 on it, out of 10 cards. It can happen, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Rolling an even number on a dice is …
c: more likely than rolling an odd number
less likely than rolling an odd number
as likely as rolling an odd number
items.e: Even numbers: 2, 4, 6 (3 faces). Odd numbers: 1, 3, 5 (3 faces). 3 and 3 are the same, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Aarav rolls a dice. Which is most likely?
items.e: Less than 5: 1, 2, 3, 4 (4 faces). A 6 is 1 face, a 1 or a 2 is 2 faces, and 7 is impossible. 4 faces is the most, so a number less than 5 is most likely.

items.q: Leo spins this spinner. Which outcome is impossible?
items.e: The spinner has 1, 2, 3 and 4. There is no 5, so landing on 5 is impossible.

items.q: Which is certain when you toss a coin?
c: It lands on heads or tails
items.e: Heads alone or tails alone might not happen. But the coin must land on heads or tails, so that is certain.

items.q: Rolling a 3 or a 4 on a dice is …
items.e: Only 2 of the 6 faces (3 and 4) work. 4 faces do not. It can happen, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Which colour came up most often?
c: they all came up the same
items.e: Red: 1 group of 5 and 4 more = 9. Blue: 7. Yellow: 4. Red has the most tally marks.

items.q: How many times did Mia spin altogether?
items.e: Add the tallies: 9 + 7 + 4 = 20.

items.q: How many more times did red come up than yellow?
items.e: Red 9, yellow 4. How many more means subtract: 9 − 4 = 5.

items.q: Jack spins this spinner 20 times. Which result would be most surprising?
items.e: Half the spinner is red and half is blue, so you expect about 10 of each. Results near 10 are normal. Red every single time is possible, but very unlikely.

items.q: William spins this spinner 20 times. Which result is most likely?
items.e: 3 of the 4 equal sections are blue, so blue should come up about 3 times as often as red. Blue 15 and red 5 fits best. The results can change a little each time.

items.q: Charlotte tosses a coin 10 times and gets 6 heads and 4 tails. She tosses it 10 more times. What will happen?
c: The results may be different this time
She will get 6 tails and 4 heads
items.e: Chance results change each time. She might get 6 heads again, or 5, or 3. We cannot know for sure.

items.q: Which number did Oliver roll most often?
items.e: Find the biggest number in the Times row: 7. That is under the number 5. (6 is the biggest number on the dice, not the most rolled.)

items.q: Oliver says 5 is the easiest number to roll, because it came up most. Is he right?
c: No, each number is equally likely
No, 4 is the easiest to roll
Yes, 5 will come up most every time
No, 6 is the easiest to roll
items.e: Each face of a dice has the same chance. Results vary: next time a different number may come up most.

items.q: Cooper picks a counter from a bag, looks at it and puts it back. He does this 20 times. He gets red 17 times and blue 3 times. Which bag did he most likely use?
items.e: Red came up much more often than blue, so the bag probably has many more red counters. It cannot be 10 red and 0 blue, because then blue would be impossible, and he picked blue 3 times.

items.q: Ava’s spinner has 4 equal sections. Which spinner did she most likely use?
items.e: Green came up 14 times and purple 6 times. Green came up much more often, so green probably covers more of the spinner. With 4 purple sections, green would be impossible.

items.q: Isla tosses a coin 4 times and gets heads every time. What about the next toss?
c: Heads and tails are still equally likely
items.e: A coin does not remember what happened before. Every toss, heads and tails are equally likely.

items.q: At the school fete, 100 raffle tickets are sold. Ava buys 1 ticket. Ava winning the raffle is …
items.e: Ava has only 1 of the 100 tickets. She could win, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Ethan’s family buys 95 of the 100 raffle tickets. Ethan’s family winning the raffle is …
items.e: 95 of the 100 tickets are theirs, so it is likely. It is not certain, because 5 tickets belong to other people.

items.q: Matilda has 10 animal cards face down: 7 kangaroo cards and 3 koala cards. She turns over one card. Getting a koala card is …
items.e: Only 3 of the 10 cards are koalas, and 7 are kangaroos. A koala can happen, but it is unlikely.

items.q: Kai’s class has 26 students. Each student puts their name in a hat, and the teacher picks one. Picking the name of a student in Kai’s class is …
items.e: Every name in the hat belongs to a student in the class, so it is certain.

items.q: Kai’s class of 26 students puts their names in a hat. The teacher picks one name. Picking Kai’s name is …
items.e: Kai’s name is only 1 of the 26 names. It could be picked, but it is unlikely.

items.q: The school canteen has 20 icy poles in a box: 18 orange and 2 lemon. Liam takes one without looking. Getting an orange icy pole is …
items.e: 18 of the 20 icy poles are orange, so orange is likely. It is not certain, because there are 2 lemon ones.

items.q: Zara rolls a dice 12 times. She gets a 6 three times. How many times did she not get a 6?
items.e: Not a 6 means all the other rolls: 12 − 3 = 9.

items.q: Year 3 tossed a coin 50 times. They got 27 heads and 23 tails. Which sentence is true?
c: Heads is more likely than tails
Heads and tails came up about the same
items.e: 27 and 23 are close. Heads and tails are equally likely, and results vary a little each time.

items.q: Chloe spins a spinner 20 times. She gets red 8 times, blue 5 times and yellow the rest of the time. How many times did she get yellow?
items.e: Step 1: red and blue: 8 + 5 = 13. Step 2: 20 − 13 = 7 times yellow.
